nobox.final_span:
tucked under his pocket a toothbrush and a Slinky from the National Museum of American History.
Armstrong detached the toothbrush from its box and noticed an inscription on the way to the moon. It honored President Harry S. Truman, who later donated the boxed brush to the Museum when he lost a tooth. The note read “Give a man a toothbrush and you feed his spirit.” Armstrong then placed the toothbrush back where it had been.
On the return trip, Armstrong requested that Buzz Aldrin, his fellow crew member and pilot, take a good look at the moon. Aldrin remembers getting the message—teasingly, as Armstrong was fond of doing—that Armstrong wanted him to have a good view, if for no other reason than to send back a photo showing the signatures of the astronaut who beat the Russians to the moon, “and also Mr. Truman, a few things...”
Both Truman and Armstrong hailed from the Midwest, with Truman being from Missouri and Armstrong from Ohio. Both men had a fondness for the Midwest and expressed firm views on farming technology. In addition to serving as president, Truman also worked as a farmer during his lifetime. He likely chose to donate toothbrushes as dentifrice was markedly missing from early flight menus. But he also understood America's military service members—included in the toothbrush packaging was a veteran of World War I who worked to introduce oral hygiene practices to the wartime generation, ensuring that service members reaped benefits from accessible and effective tooth-cleaning tools on the American frontlines. Although Truman started his military service in 1917 by serving in Congress, he did not illusion himself about missing out on the fun. He participated in leading America into World War I, and fought alongside his military colleagues for the Allies.
